title: Future-Proofing Legal Ops: AI Literacy, Innovation and Augmentation (Meredith Kildow, President Consilio)
author: Meredith Kildow

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: Kildow does not address the justice gap or show that AI-driven productivity expands meaningful legal help. She instead focuses on commercial in-house legal operations, advocating augmentation and adoption for low-risk, high-volume departmental work; this reinforces the distinction between uptake and transformation but redirects the discussion toward enterprise efficiency.
qs: I do think that LegalOps teams are going to have to incorporate it into how they work, right?

And I think that there's the potential to be more effective and more efficient and to take a lot of the more low-risk, the higher-volume, you know, the tasks throughout legal departments that are ripe for this kind of disruption and really embrace that.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The excerpt is only a contact invitation and sign-off. It provides no substantive claim or evidence about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation, leadership, user feedback, or autonomous workflows, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports task-level AI adoption in document review and interest in upstream investigations, consistent with bounded substitution and workflow-specific value. But it provides no measured productivity, savings or staffing effects, and the job-displacement question is left unanswered, so its position on whether complementarity will reshape staffing cannot be determined.
qs: I mean, interestingly, where we get the most sort of actual projects or people utilizing it does, you know, still live in the review space, where we get the most inquiries and where people want to talk about it the most, is upstream of that in sort of an investigations.
Do you sense a fear within the LegalOps community that AIs, like other jobs, are going to take their job?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Kildow accepts the need for selective, use-case-specific deployment and materially extends it with a concrete delivery model: flexible multi-model architecture, controlled infrastructure, targeted workflows, and client-led proofs of concept. Her emphasis on workflow-level ROI and differing model performance aligns closely with the cluster’s jagged-capability and operating-model claims, though she provides limited discussion of human verification.
qs: Like we are able to tap into different models because we found that depending on what the use case is, different models behave differently and have better outcomes.

So whether that's giving them that space in the Innovation Lab to sort of create and test, or really all the hundreds of POCs that we've done with clients, or even have clients that we're co-developing products with around very specific use cases for shared strategic clients or things like that.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Kildow supports the cluster’s emphasis on client outcomes, buyer-side incentives and experimentation as adoption drivers. Her observations also fit the cluster’s caution that implementation remains selective and workflow-specific, concentrated in document review with interest moving upstream into investigations; she does not substantively address pricing pressure, apprenticeship or staffing succession.
qs: Everybody touching the business understands what the client wants, understands what the best outcome looks like.
You know, we now have five or six pretty robust AI tools within our ecosystem, all at the response of where clients were pushing us.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Kildow supports the cluster’s practical, bounded-adoption thesis: current use is concentrated in document review and upstream investigations, while buyer-side cost pressure drives demand for coherent workflows with demonstrable efficiency and ROI. She emphasizes matter-level experimentation rather than autonomous legal delivery or adoption for its own sake.
qs: I mean, interestingly, where we get the most sort of actual projects or people utilizing it does, you know, still live in the review space, where we get the most inquiries and where people want to talk about it the most, is upstream of that in sort of an investigations.

But how you can get to a workflow that makes sense, that you're actually seeing efficiency from it, and at the same time, our clients have a lot of pressure, I think, coming from their own leadership to show ROI and efficiency through AI usage, right?

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Kildow supports the cluster’s framing of AI adoption as leadership-backed, hands-on organisational experimentation centred on concrete client use cases rather than technology acquisition alone. Her evidence is observational and programme-based, however, and she leaves the scale and form of eventual change uncertain rather than demonstrating transformation outcomes.
qs: I think it varies organization to organization, but I do think generally this kind of adoption is coming all the way from the top in these organizations.

So whether that's giving them that space in the Innovation Lab to sort of create and test, or really all the hundreds of POCs that we've done with clients, or even have clients that we're co-developing products with around very specific use cases for shared strategic clients or things like that.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s emphasis on coordinated, technology-enabled service delivery and on separating commercial efficiency claims from demonstrated AI outcomes. Its team-alignment rationale is concrete, while the Percipient claims remain promotional and the interviewer’s demand for present use reinforces scrutiny of AI hype; it does not itself demonstrate routine relief creating strategic capacity.
qs: And I think one of the things about bringing these two parts of the org under me that was important was that we collaborate as teams, because I think often the best client delivery is when all of those people are aligned, right?
But what are you really seeing, you internally, what you guys are doing, but clients, how is it really actually being used today?

kp.k: Cost pressures drive legal departments toward AI
kp.d: Kildow reports that clients face leadership pressure to demonstrate ROI and efficiency from AI while continuing to manage legal risk. She describes a fragmented supplier ecosystem in which identifying an effective workflow remains challenging. These are practitioner observations about client demand, not quantified findings about achieved savings.
qs: So I think our clients really view it as both a problem and a solution, and are looking for folks like us to really help them navigate, which feels like a very disparate and challenging ecosystem around AI right now.
our clients have a lot of pressure, I think, coming from their own leadership to show ROI and efficiency through AI usage
And legal departments everywhere, you know, being a cost center, I think, feel that pressure.

kp.k: Review leads actual use; investigations attract strongest interest
kp.d: Kildow distinguishes Consilio's actual AI projects, concentrated in document review, from inquiries concentrated upstream in investigations and fact-finding. Clients want earlier insights into large datasets and less data moving downstream. She also identifies contracts as an early adoption area and growing interest among litigation teams; no measured document reduction or ROI is supplied.
qs: where we get the most sort of actual projects or people utilizing it does, you know, still live in the review space
where we get the most inquiries and where people want to talk about it the most, is upstream of that in sort of an investigations.
manage these enormous amounts of data, move less of that data downstream

kp.k: Legal operations faces augmentation rather than replacement
kp.d: Asked by host Chad Main about job loss, Kildow rejects replacement of legal operations professionals and argues that teams will need to incorporate AI into their work. She sees opportunities in low-risk, high-volume tasks and reports enthusiasm among most leaders she works with. This is her expectation and client impression, not employment evidence.
qs: No, I don't think it's going to take... I don't think it can.
I do think that LegalOps teams are going to have to incorporate it into how they work

there's the potential to be more effective and more efficient and to take a lot of the more low-risk, the higher-volume, you know, the tasks throughout legal departments that are ripe for this kind of disruption and really embrace that.

kp.k: Survey discussion mixes training and deployment measures
kp.d: Main cites a survey of 129 legal professionals in which only 10 percent reported very trained teams. Kildow instead describes last year's 10 percent as full AI deployment and reports a result 'up north of 30 percent' from Consilio's 2026 global survey, which she says covered more than 600 clients across corporations and law firms. The transcript does not reconcile the measures, so these cannot be presented as a consistent training trend. Although the document is labelled 2025, her survey reference is explicitly 2026.
qs: A survey of 129 legal professionals, only 10 percent reported that their teams are very trained on generative AI.
We just did our 2026 global survey, and I think it was more than 600 of our clients, both corporations and law firms globally.
From that 10 percent full deployment of AI stat from last year, we're seeing that now in this result up north of 30 percent.

kp.k: AI literacy combines technical and substantive expertise
kp.d: Drawing on Consilio's proofs of concept and projects over roughly the preceding year, Kildow argues that AI works better when guided by people who understand both the technology and the underlying legal work, including protocols and matter merits. She positions this combined expertise as a source of provider value rather than treating literacy as software familiarity alone; no comparative performance figures are provided.
qs: the AI particularly in our space is so much more effective when there are experts and it's guided by people who not only understand the technology and the best way to make the AI work, but also understand whether it's protocols or the merits of a matter, or understand the work itself.
it's not just around the technology or the software, it's also about the work itself and bringing those two things together.

kp.k: Specialist teams and client sandboxes support experimentation
kp.d: Kildow describes building prompt-engineering and AI-specialist capacity alongside a rapid prototype team. An innovation lab established a year or 18 months earlier lets strategic corporate clients select and test technologies in Consilio's secure sandbox, including co-developing solutions for unmet needs. She says the lab is now launching for law firms. Viable prototypes pass into the regular product organization, with internal efficiency initiatives distinguished from client-driven commercial products.
qs: We have built and continue to build a large population of prompt engineers and AI specialists
We help them through a sandbox environment, test them out all within the secure environment that they already trust Consilio for.
we are informing each other, creating a lot of literacy in that way together
they are building things to a prototype spec that, you know, if viable, then get passed into our, you know, regular product organization.

kp.k: Platform flexibility addresses uncertain AI development
kp.d: Kildow presents Aurora as Consilio's digital enterprise platform combining data insights, dashboarding and an Early Case Intelligence repository powered by AI tools. Its stated design allows multiple toolsets, review platforms and language models rather than dependence on one model. She attributes this approach to uncertainty about future technology and observed differences in model outcomes across use cases.
qs: we don't know what is going to happen with AI, right? And we don't feel like anybody does.
everything that we've built has been built so that they can utilize multiple tool sets.
we are able to tap into different models because we found that depending on what the use case is, different models behave differently and have better outcomes.

kp.k: AI offerings span investigation, relevance and privilege workflows
kp.d: Kildow reports five or six robust AI tools developed in response to client requests. She identifies AI investigate for upstream fact-finding, guided AI review for relevance, PrivGen for privilege identification and PrivLog Descriptions. She also describes a TrueLaw suite acquired about six months earlier with narratives and ELM products delivered through SaaS. These are descriptions of offerings and claimed utility, not independent evaluations.
qs: we now have five or six pretty robust AI tools within our ecosystem, all at the response of where clients were pushing us.
We also have guided AI review, which is really around relevance. We have PrivGen, which is around priv identification.
We have PrivLog Descriptions is another place that we've found AI to have really good outcomes for us.
It’s a true SaaS model today.

kp.k: Private infrastructure and cost control differentiate provider offerings
kp.d: Kildow contrasts Consilio's flexible toolset with platform-specific AI offered by Relativity, Reveal and Everlaw. She says Consilio runs its tools in a controlled private-cloud environment for clients unwilling to send material to public-cloud services. She also argues that this architecture enables cost control and reports vendors changing pricing models because cost has obstructed adoption. No price comparisons or security assessments are supplied.
qs: We built them to be flexible.
we harness the power of large language models, but we do that in a much more controlled private cloud environment.
And then the other piece of that is we think it allows us to control for cost.
I think we see a movement with the software vendors today that they're figuring out that cost was an obstacle for folks. And I think you see them changing pricing models.

kp.k: Executive mandates coexist with demand for hands-on testing
kp.d: Kildow reports top-down adoption directives, including some client budgets available only for AI-enabled purchases. Alongside those mandates, she observes genuine curiosity in firms and corporations and a desire to understand effects on actual matters through experimentation. She cites hundreds of client proofs of concept and some product co-development, without reporting success rates.
qs: I do think generally this kind of adoption is coming all the way from the top in these organizations.
if it does not harness some sort of AI technology or software, they cannot utilize that budget for it.
people want to know how is this going to impact the matter? What is the change going to look like?
all the hundreds of POCs that we've done with clients

kp.k: Client-led delivery aligns service efficiency and revenue growth
kp.d: Kildow argues that listening to clients should guide both product development and delivery, with different approaches for sectors, law firms and corporate legal departments. She describes aligning revenue and delivery teams around desired client outcomes as compatible with growth and efficiency. This is a management approach supporting Consilio's technology strategy, not a measured AI productivity result.
qs: everything we do, we really try to listen to the clients
understanding the nuance of that, helping the teams craft bespoke and custom delivery is part of I view the job, but at the same time, that is also how we grow the revenue in the business.
Everybody touching the business understands what the client wants, understands what the best outcome looks like.

kp.k: Faster adoption suggests change, but outcomes remain uncertain
kp.d: In response to a five-year forecast question, Kildow contrasts current AI adoption with earlier expectations surrounding technology-assisted review. She anticipates tangible changes because adoption feels faster, but explicitly declines to specify their form and stresses month-to-month uncertainty. This is a qualified prediction rather than evidence of a particular future workforce or business model.
qs: I think that the adoption and the speed to adoption that we're seeing with AI feels very different.
So I do think that we're going to see some pretty tangible changes.
I think we don't even know what those changes will really look like.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Meredith Kildow describes expanding but uneven AI adoption, especially in document review, and predicts augmentation of legal operations rather than replacement. She presents expert guidance, experimentation and flexible technology as important to achieving benefits.
pts.d: Kildow makes the following claims: (1) Corporate leadership is pressuring legal departments to demonstrate AI-related ROI and efficiency, sometimes through budgets restricted to AI use. AI is a potential means of reducing costs while continuing to manage risk, not a guaranteed saving. (2) Contract work was an early adoption area; litigation teams are now exploring potential returns. At Consilio, actual AI projects remain concentrated in document review, whereas the most inquiries concern upstream investigations, fact-finding and reducing the data sent downstream. (3) She does not expect AI to take legal operations professionals' jobs, but says teams must incorporate it into their work; low-risk, high-volume tasks offer opportunities for greater effectiveness and efficiency. (4) She reports full AI deployment above 30 percent in a recent client survey, compared with a stated 10 percent the previous year. (5) AI in Consilio's work is more effective when guided by people combining technical knowledge with understanding of the legal work, protocols and matter merits. (6) Consilio's innovation lab and client co-development create AI literacy through practical experimentation and can generate products where existing offerings do not address client needs. (7) Different models perform differently by use case; Consilio therefore offers multiple tools and models rather than committing to one. She reports good outcomes from AI-generated privilege-log descriptions and argues that flexible, controlled private-cloud deployment addresses some clients' confidentiality preferences and helps control costs. She also observes vendors changing pricing as cost proves an adoption obstacle. (8) She expects tangible changes over the next five years because current AI adoption feels faster than technology-assisted review adoption, but expressly declines to predict their specific form.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists mainly of Kildow's operational experience, client interactions and proofs of concept, plus a reported client survey; no quantified performance or cost-saving results are supplied.
pts.d: Kildow draws on her position overseeing Consilio's revenue and delivery operations, client requests, projects, hundreds of proofs of concept, a client summit and co-development work. Her claims about expert guidance, model differences and privilege-log results are experience-based; she supplies no benchmark scores, accuracy rates, measured savings or comparative study design. Her adoption statistic comes from what she calls Consilio's '2026 global survey' of more than 600 corporate and law-firm clients globally. She describes deployment as rising from 10 percent to above 30 percent, but provides no methodology or explanation of comparability. Importantly, the interviewer's preceding 10 percent figure concerned training in a survey of 129 professionals, whereas Kildow describes her baseline as full deployment: these are different measures and should not be conflated. The document is labelled 2025 despite her reference to a 2026 survey. Her rejection of legal-operations job replacement and five-year outlook are judgments, not findings supported by workforce data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern current practice or the preceding year; benefits are conditional on suitable tasks, expertise and workable deployment. The five-year forecast is explicitly uncertain.
pts.d: The review-versus-investigations distinction describes actual use versus interest at the time of the interview, not completed transformation of investigations. Kildow situates observations about expert-guided AI in projects over roughly the prior year and client demand for hands-on testing over the prior nine to twelve months. The corporate innovation lab was established approximately twelve to eighteen months earlier, with a law-firm version launching at interview time. The deployment comparison is framed as the latest survey versus 'last year,' without a reconciled publication chronology. Efficiency is described as potential, especially for low-risk, high-volume tasks, and depends on incorporating AI into workflows and combining technological and substantive expertise. Platform flexibility is justified by uncertainty about future models and tools; private-cloud deployment responds to particular clients' preferences, not a stated universal requirement. In response to a five-year question, Kildow predicts tangible change but emphasizes month-to-month developments and uncertainty about what those changes will be.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, legal operations teams, law firms, and legal-service providers and vendors serving review, investigations and related workflows.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments face top-down cost and ROI expectations while retaining risk-management responsibilities; dedicated AI budgets can shape procurement. Legal operations professionals are positioned as adopters whose work may become more effective, rather than as a workforce Kildow expects AI to replace. Contract and litigation teams encounter different adoption stages, with review users already undertaking projects and investigation teams exploring earlier insights and reduced downstream data volumes. Corporate and law-firm clients gain opportunities to test tools, influence product development and build AI literacy, initially through a lab for strategic corporate clients and subsequently a law-firm offering. Consilio, a legal-services provider with technology offerings, is developing prompt-engineering and AI-specialist capabilities and positioning combined technical and legal-work expertise as added client value. Software vendors face pricing pressure, while clients concerned about public-cloud processing are offered a controlled private-cloud alternative. The source does not make claims about access to justice, public legal need, associate staffing structures or profession-wide employment totals.
